claim: NLRP3 inflammasome activation and complement-mediated inflammation have been implicated in promoting choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: NLRP3 inflammasome activation and complement-mediated inflammation have been implicated in promoting choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), but central questions regarding their contributions to AMD pathogenesis remain unanswered.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature in the field, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: NLRP3 inflammasome activation in non-RPE cells but not in RPE cells promotes CNV.
source: Here we show in a neovascular AMD mouse model that NLRP3 inflammasome activation in non-RPE cells but not in RPE cells promotes CNV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study using VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice and VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice, showing similar CNV reduction in both groups.

claim: Both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent inflammasome activation mechanisms induce CNV.
source: We demonstrate that both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent inflammasome activation mechanisms induce CNV.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing caspase-1 p10 activation in VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice despite absence of NLRP3 protein.

claim: Complement and inflammasomes promote CNV through independent mechanisms.
source: Finally, we find that complement and inflammasomes promote CNV through independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that VegfahyperC3-/- mice have reduced CNV but still show inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid lysates.

claim: Combination therapies targeting inflammasomes and complement may offer synergistic benefits to inhibit CNV.
source: Our findings uncover an unexpected role of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes for CNV and suggest that combination therapies targeting inflammasomes and complement may offer synergistic benefits to inhibit CNV.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the finding that complement and inflammasomes act through independent mechanisms.

claim: Canonical inflammasome activation is initiated by cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) when exposed to specific triggers.
source: Canonical inflammasome activation is initiated by cytosolic pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) when exposed to specific triggers (either microbe-derived pathogen-associated molecular patterns [PAMPs] or host-derived danger-associated molecular patterns [DAMPs]).
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about inflammasome biology.

claim: PRRs include the family of NOD-like receptors (NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRP6, NLRC4), or AIM2, IFI16, and pyrin.
source: These PRRs include the family of NOD-like receptors (NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRP6, NLRC4), or AIM2, IFI16, and pyrin.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about PRR families.

claim: Upon sensing specific stimuli, PRRs oligomerize and form together with the ASC adaptor protein scaffolds that activate caspase-1.
source: Upon sensing specific stimuli, PRRs oligomerize and form together with the ASC adaptor protein scaffolds that activate caspase-1.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about inflammasome activation mechanisms.

claim: Autoproteolytic activation of pro-caspase-1 leads to the release of effector domains caspase-1 p10 and p20, which are required for the proteolytic processing of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active mature forms.
source: This results in autoproteolytic activation of pro-caspase-1 that leads to the release of their effector domains caspase-1 p10 and p20, which are required for the proteolytic processing of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active mature forms that promote inflammation and angiogenesis (Guo et al., 2015; Latz et al., 2013; Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A non-canonical inflammasome has been described in which bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activates caspase-11 (caspase-4/–5 in humans) to induce pyroptotic cell death.
source: Of note, a non-canonical inflammasome has been described in which bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activates caspase-11 (caspase-4/–5 in humans) to induce pyroptotic cell death (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: Various stimuli that are well-established risk factors for AMD, including increased oxidative stress or lipid accumulations, are known activators of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: The reason for this very narrow focus on NLRP3 as a PRR that initiates inflammasome activation in AMD is that various stimuli that are well-established risk factors for AMD, including increased oxidative stress or lipid accumulations, are known activators of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Guo et al., 2015; Latz et al., 2013; Schroder and Tschopp, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IL-1β is known to stimulate inflammatory angiogenesis.
source: This has led to the assumption that AMD risk factors promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which further exacerbates AMD pathologies through activation of proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β that is known to stimulate inflammatory angiogenesis (Lavalette et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lavalette et al., 2011.

claim: NLRP3 is expressed in RPE cells in human non-exudative AMD.
source: A study by Tarallo et al reported that NLRP3 is expressed in RPE cells in human non-exudative AMD and that targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome or IL-18 could inhibit RPE-degeneration (Tarallo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tarallo et al., 2012.

claim: Targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome or IL-18 could inhibit RPE-degeneration.
source: A study by Tarallo et al reported that NLRP3 is expressed in RPE cells in human non-exudative AMD and that targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome or IL-18 could inhibit RPE-degeneration (Tarallo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tarallo et al., 2012.

claim: NLRP3 inflammasome activation occurs in macrophages and results in IL-18 activation that inhibits laser-induced CNV.
source: A study by Doyle et al reported that NLRP3 inflammasome activation occurs in macrophages and results in IL-18 activation that inhibits laser-induced CNV (Doyle et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doyle et al., 2012.

claim: Multiple other groups could not detect an effect of IL-18 on laser-induced CNV.
source: Moreover, multiple other groups could not detect an effect of IL-18 on laser-induced CNV (Hirano et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hirano et al., 2014.

claim: Increased VEGF-A levels in the RPE resulted in increased inflammasome activation products in RPE/choroids of Vegfahyper mice.
source: We also tested the role of IL-18 in a novel genetic mouse model of neovascular AMD, Vegfahyper mice, in which we observed that increased VEGF-A levels in the RPE resulted in increased inflammasome activation products in RPE/choroids of these mice as well as in spontaneous CNV formation in an age-dependent manner without experimental injury (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Vegfahyper mice form spontaneous CNV in an age-dependent manner without experimental injury.
source: We also tested the role of IL-18 in a novel genetic mouse model of neovascular AMD, Vegfahyper mice, in which we observed that increased VEGF-A levels in the RPE resulted in increased inflammasome activation products in RPE/choroids of these mice as well as in spontaneous CNV formation in an age-dependent manner without experimental injury (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Inactivation of Il18 does not significantly affect CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice.
source: We showed that inactivation of Il18 does not significantly affect CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice, whereas inactivation of Nlrp3, Casp1, or Il1r potently inhibits CNV lesion formation in these mice (Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Inactivation of Nlrp3, Casp1, or Il1r potently inhibits CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice.
source: We showed that inactivation of Il18 does not significantly affect CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice, whereas inactivation of Nlrp3, Casp1, or Il1r potently inhibits CNV lesion formation in these mice (Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Activation of IL-1β through the NLRP3 inflammasome promotes VEGF-A-induced CNV in mice, whereas IL-18 has no major effect.
source: These findings provide evidence that activation of IL-1β through the NLRP3 inflammasome promotes VEGF-A-induced CNV in mice, whereas IL-18 has no major effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of Il18 versus Nlrp3/Casp1/Il1r inactivation.

claim: Inflammasome activation in RPE/choroids of Vegfahyper mice was associated with the accumulation of known triggers of the inflammasome in CNV lesions, including increased markers of oxidative stress and sub-RPE lipid deposits.
source: Notably, inflammasome activation in RPE/choroids of Vegfahyper mice was associated with the accumulation of known triggers of the inflammasome in CNV lesions, including increased markers of oxidative stress and sub-RPE lipid deposits (Marneros, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marneros, 2013.

claim: Spontaneous CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice can be accurately quantified already at a young age (at 6 weeks of age).
source: In this Vegfahyper mouse model of AMD, spontaneous CNV lesion formation can be accurately quantified already at a young age (here quantified at 6 weeks of age).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: CNV lesions in Vegfahyper mice enlarge with progressive age and can merge with adjacent lesions to form larger confluent areas of CNV.
source: These CNV lesions enlarge with progressive age and can merge with adjacent lesions to form larger confluent areas of CNV (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016), similarly as observed in human neovascular AMD where multiple adjacent ingrowth sites of neovessels from choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane can merge to form larger CNV lesions (Grossniklaus and Green, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In human neovascular AMD, multiple adjacent ingrowth sites of neovessels from choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane can merge to form larger CNV lesions.
source: These CNV lesions enlarge with progressive age and can merge with adjacent lesions to form larger confluent areas of CNV (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016), similarly as observed in human neovascular AMD where multiple adjacent ingrowth sites of neovessels from choriocapillaris through Bruch's membrane can merge to form larger CNV lesions (Grossniklaus and Green, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grossniklaus and Green, 2004.

claim: NLRP3 protein was not detected in the RPE of human eyes with AMD in a recent study.
source: For example, NLRP3 protein was not detected in the RPE of human eyes with AMD in a recent study that tested only a limited number of antibodies, questioning whether inflammasome activation occurs in the RPE at all (Kosmidou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kosmidou et al., 2018.

claim: The study by Kosmidou et al. did not investigate whether actual inflammasome activation occurs in the RPE.
source: However, this study did not investigate whether actual inflammasome activation occurs in the RPE (cleaved caspase-1 p10 or p20 levels or IL-1β secretion were not assessed, which serve as inflammasome activation markers) (Kosmidou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of the cited study.

claim: Other studies found evidence for inflammasome activation or specifically for NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human RPE cells.
source: By contrast, other studies found evidence for inflammasome activation or specifically for NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human RPE cells (Hollborn et al., 2018; Tseng et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Sub-lytic effects of the complement pathway activation product C5b-9 can induce NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages.
source: Notably, recent in vitro studies suggested that sub-lytic effects of the complement pathway activation product C5b-9 (also called membrane attack complex) can induce NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages (Laudisi et al., 2013; Suresh et al., 2016; Triantafilou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The complement activation product C3a has been shown to activate the inflammasome in macrophages in vitro.
source: Moreover, the complement activation product C3a has been shown to activate the inflammasome in macrophages in vitro as well (Asgari et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Asgari et al., 2013.

claim: Complement-mediated inflammation occurs in AMD and has been linked to AMD disease progression.
source: As complement-mediated inflammation occurs in AMD and has been linked to AMD disease progression, this raises the question of whether complement activation products may promote AMD pathologies in part by triggering inflammasome activation in AMD lesions (Gehrs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gehrs et al., 2010.

claim: Accumulation of complement C5b-9 occurs in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice.
source: Vegfahyper mice offer the opportunity to test the roles of complement pathway activation for inflammasome activation and CNV formation, as we observed accumulation of complement C5b-9 in CNV lesions of these mice (Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marneros, 2016.

claim: The caspase-11 non-canonical inflammasome does not affect CNV.
source: Here our data provide important answers to these key questions: (1) we show that NLRP3 inflammasome activation mainly in non-RPE cells and not in RPE cells promotes CNV; (2) we demonstrate that not only NLRP3-dependent but also NLRP3-independent inflammasome activation promotes CNV; (3) we show that the caspase-11 non-canonical inflammasome does not affect CNV; and (4) we provide evidence that complement pathway activation promotes CNV largely independently of inflammasome activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no difference in CNV between VegfahyperCasp11-/- and Vegfahyper mice.

claim: Complement pathway activation promotes CNV largely independently of inflammasome activation.
source: Here our data provide important answers to these key questions: (1) we show that NLRP3 inflammasome activation mainly in non-RPE cells and not in RPE cells promotes CNV; (2) we demonstrate that not only NLRP3-dependent but also NLRP3-independent inflammasome activation promotes CNV; (3) we show that the caspase-11 non-canonical inflammasome does not affect CNV; and (4) we provide evidence that complement pathway activation promotes CNV largely independently of inflammasome activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that VegfahyperC3-/- mice have reduced CNV but still show inflammasome activation.

claim: Combining therapies that target both the canonical inflammasome as well as the complement pathway likely offer synergistic therapeutic benefits for patients with neovascular AMD.
source: These findings have significant translational relevance and suggest that combining therapies that target both the canonical inflammasome as well as the complement pathway likely offer synergistic therapeutic benefits for patients with neovascular AMD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the finding that complement and inflammasomes act through independent mechanisms.

claim: At sites devoid of CNV lesions, the RPE and retina appear morphologically normal in 6-weeks-old Vegfahyper mice.
source: At sites devoid of CNV lesions, the RPE and retina appear morphologically normal in 6-weeks-old Vegfahyper mice (Figure 1A and B; Marneros, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A and B and citation to Marneros, 2013.

claim: In aged Vegfahyper mice RPE cells become atrophic and the photoreceptor layer of the retina is attenuated.
source: By contrast, in aged Vegfahyper mice RPE cells become atrophic and the photoreceptor layer of the retina is attenuated as well, resembling pathologies seen in nonexudative AMD (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A > 2 fold increase in p10 levels relative to WT (normalized to β-actin levels) are observed at 6 weeks of age in RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice.
source: A > 2 fold increase in p10 levels relative to WT (normalized to β-actin levels) are observed at 6 weeks of age in RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice and VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice show significantly decreased CNV lesion numbers compared to Vegfahyper mice.
source: VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice (group 2) and VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice (group 3) show significantly decreased CNV lesion numbers compared to Vegfahyper mice (group 1), but no significant difference in CNV lesion sizes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice have fewer CNV lesions than VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice or VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice.
source: VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice (group 4) have fewer CNV lesions than VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice or VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The constitutively active Nlrp3A350V/A350V allele in the RPE does not promote CNV lesion formation.
source: The similar effect on CNV lesion number reduction in VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice and VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice shows that the constitutively active Nlrp3A350V/A350V allele in the RPE does not promote CNV lesion formation, whereas NLRP3 inflammasome inactivation in non-RPE cells potently inhibits CNV lesion induction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the similar CNV reduction in both mouse groups.

claim: NLRP3 inflammasome inactivation in non-RPE cells potently inhibits CNV lesion induction.
source: The similar effect on CNV lesion number reduction in VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice and VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice shows that the constitutively active Nlrp3A350V/A350V allele in the RPE does not promote CNV lesion formation, whereas NLRP3 inflammasome inactivation in non-RPE cells potently inhibits CNV lesion induction.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the similar CNV reduction in both mouse groups.

claim: F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions have high levels of caspase-1 protein.
source: F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions have high levels of caspase-1 protein
evidence: This is a section heading that summarizes findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: Strong immunolabeling for caspase-1 or its activation product p10 occurs predominantly in F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice, whereas no strong immunolabeling was detected in their RPE cells.
source: We observed strong immunolabeling for caspase-1 or its activation product p10 predominantly in F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice, whereas no strong immunolabeling was detected in their RPE cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: A subset of F4/80+ cells that infiltrate CNV lesions in Vegfahyper mice and showed caspase-1 p10 labeling also expressed the microglia marker P2RY12.
source: Notably, we observed that a subset of F4/80+ cells that infiltrate CNV lesions in Vegfahyper mice and showed caspase-1 p10 labeling also expressed the microglia marker P2RY12, whereas P2RY12+ microglia in the retina at sites devoid of CNV lesions did not label for caspase-1 p10 (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inflammasome activation occurs in both macrophages (F4/80+P2RY12neg) and in activated retinal microglia cells (F4/80+P2RY12+) that infiltrate CNV lesions in Vegfahyper mice.
source: This suggests that inflammasome activation occurs in both macrophages (F4/80+P2RY12neg) and in activated retinal microglia cells (F4/80+P2RY12+) that infiltrate CNV lesions in these mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunolabeling data showing F4/80+, p10+, and P2RY12+ cells.

claim: Inflammasome activation primarily in F4/80+ cells and not in RPE cells drives CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice.
source: Together with our observation that NLRP3 inflammasome activation mainly in non-RPE cells promotes CNV, these data suggest that inflammasome activation primarily in F4/80+ cells and not in RPE cells drives CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including cell-specific Nlrp3 activation and immunolabeling data.

claim: F4/80+ cells infiltrate the subretinal space at the site of RPE barrier breakdown in Vegfahyper mice and are spatiotemporally associated with activation of retinal glia cells when CNV lesions form at that site.
source: Indeed, F4/80+ cells infiltrate the subretinal space at the site of RPE barrier breakdown in Vegfahyper mice and are spatiotemporally associated with activation of retinal glia cells when CNV lesions form at that site (Marneros, 2013), suggesting that these cells are important for the initiation of CNV lesion formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marneros, 2013.

claim: Ablation of macrophages inhibits laser-induced CNV.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we and others found that ablation of macrophages (by using either LysMCre/+iDTR mice treated with diphtheria toxin or using clodronate liposomes) inhibits laser-induced CNV (Espinosa-Heidmann et al., 2003; Marneros, 2013; Sakurai et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An increase in caspase-1 inflammasome activation (increased cleaved caspase-1 p10 levels) compared to WT littermates was present already in young Vegfahyper mice.
source: We found in western blots of RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice that an increase in caspase-1 inflammasome activation (increased cleaved caspase-1 p10 levels) compared to WT littermates was present already in young mice (increased ratios of p10/β-actin band intensities in RPE/choroid lysates of 6-weeks-old Vegfahyper mice shown in Figure 1F and of 2-months-old Vegfahyper mice shown in Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 1F and 4A.

claim: The age-dependent exacerbation of AMD pathologies was associated with a steady further increase in inflammasome activation in RPE/choroids of Vegfahyper mice with age progression.
source: The age-dependent exacerbation of AMD pathologies was also associated with a steady further increase in inflammasome activation in RPE/choroids of Vegfahyper mice with age progression and aged Vegfahyper mice showed high levels of caspase-1 p10 in their RPE/choroids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NLRP3 protein is present in RPE/choroid lysates from young WT and Vegfahyper mice.
source: Western blots detected NLRP3 protein already in RPE/choroid lysates from young WT and Vegfahyper mice, whereas NLRP3 protein was absent in RPE/choroid lysates from VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: RPE/choroid lysates from VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice showed the presence of a cleaved caspase-1 p10 band despite the absence of NLRP3 protein.
source: Moreover, RPE/choroid lysates from VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice showed the presence of a cleaved caspase-1 p10 band despite the absence of NLRP3 protein, demonstrating that inflammasome activation in eyes of Vegfahyper mice is not dependent on NLRP3 and can also be mediated through other inflammasome activators/PRRs in the absence of NLRP3 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: Inflammasome activation in eyes of Vegfahyper mice is not dependent on NLRP3 and can also be mediated through other inflammasome activators/PRRs in the absence of NLRP3.
source: Moreover, RPE/choroid lysates from VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice showed the presence of a cleaved caspase-1 p10 band despite the absence of NLRP3 protein, demonstrating that inflammasome activation in eyes of Vegfahyper mice is not dependent on NLRP3 and can also be mediated through other inflammasome activators/PRRs in the absence of NLRP3 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the western blot data showing p10 in the absence of NLRP3.

claim: Caspase-1 activation increased in VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice in an age-dependent manner similarly as in Vegfahyper mice.
source: Caspase-1 activation increased in VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice in an age-dependent manner similarly as in Vegfahyper mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Strong caspase-1 immunolabeling occurred in F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions of VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice to a similar extent as seen in Vegfahyper mice.
source: This is also consistent with our observation that strong caspase-1 immunolabeling occurred in F4/80+ cells in CNV lesions of VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice to a similar extent as seen in Vegfahyper mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid tissues of Vegfahyper mice can occur through both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent mechanisms.
source: Together with the observation of reduced CNV lesion formation in VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice compared to Vegfahyper mice, these data suggest that inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid tissues of Vegfahyper mice can occur through both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including CNV reduction in Nlrp3-/- mice and persistent p10 in these mice.

claim: Vegfahyper mice that lack caspase-1/caspase-11 exhibit a stronger reduction in CNV lesion numbers compared to Vegfahyper mice that lack only NLRP3.
source: These findings are in accordance with our observation that Vegfahyper mice that lack caspase-1/caspase-11 (and, thus, lack all canonical and non-canonical inflammasomes) exhibit a stronger reduction in CNV lesion numbers compared to Vegfahyper mice that lack only NLRP3 (Figure 2B and C; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and C and citation to Marneros, 2016.

claim: CNV lesions were fewer and smaller in size in VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice when compared to VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice or VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice.
source: In fact, CNV lesions were fewer and smaller in size (decreased lesion formation as well as a decreased lesion growth) in VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice when compared to VegfahyperNlrp3-/- mice or VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Mice that lack Casp1 have an incidental inactivating mutation in Casp11.
source: Mice that lack Casp1 (thus, lacking all canonical inflammasomes as caspase-1 is a required component of all inflammasomes) have also an incidental inactivating mutation in Casp11 (they are therefore double KOs for both caspase-1 and caspase-11 [referred to as VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/-mice; Kayagaki et al., 2011].
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice have no caspase-1 protein.
source: We show that these VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice have indeed no caspase-1 protein [thus, no inflammasome activity], as no pro-caspase-1 nor any caspase-1 p10 can be detected in western blots of RPE/choroid lysates from these mice [Figure 4B]).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lack of caspase-11 does not reduce inflammasome activation (caspase-1 p10 levels are not diminished in RPE/choroid lysates of VegfahyperCasp11-/- mice).
source: We show in this western blot that, indeed, lack of caspase-11 does not reduce inflammasome activation (caspase-1 p10 levels are not diminished in RPE/choroid lysates of VegfahyperCasp11-/- mice) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lack of caspase-11 does not affect CNV lesion numbers or sizes.
source: Consistent with this finding, lack of caspase-11 does also not affect CNV lesion numbers or sizes (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: Caspase-11-independent caspase-1 inflammasome activation that is triggered by both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent mechanisms contributes to CNV induction in Vegfahyper mice.
source: Thus, caspase-11-independent caspase-1 inflammasome activation that is triggered by both NLRP3-dependent and NLRP3-independent mechanisms contributes to CNV induction in Vegfahyper mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on Nlrp3, Casp1, and Casp11 effects on CNV.

claim: Lack of caspase-1/caspase-11 potently reduces not only CNV lesion numbers but also CNV lesion sizes.
source: Notably, lack of caspase-1/caspase-11 potently reduces not only CNV lesion numbers but also CNV lesion sizes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Complement factor H (CFH) has been shown to inhibit CD47-mediated elimination of mononuclear phagocytes that maintains homeostasis in the subretinal space.
source: Complement factor H (CFH) has been shown to inhibit CD47-mediated elimination of mononuclear phagocytes that maintains homeostasis in the subretinal space, and AMD-associated CFH variants may through this mechanism cause an accumulation of subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that promote AMD pathologies (Calippe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calippe et al., 2017.

claim: AMD-associated CFH variants may cause an accumulation of subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that promote AMD pathologies.
source: Complement factor H (CFH) has been shown to inhibit CD47-mediated elimination of mononuclear phagocytes that maintains homeostasis in the subretinal space, and AMD-associated CFH variants may through this mechanism cause an accumulation of subretinal mononuclear phagocytes that promote AMD pathologies (Calippe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calippe et al., 2017.

claim: Several human genetic studies implicated a disease-promoting role of complement-mediated inflammation for neovascular AMD.
source: Moreover, several human genetic studies implicated a disease-promoting role of complement-mediated inflammation for neovascular AMD (Gehrs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gehrs et al., 2010.

claim: Complement activation products C3a, C5a and the membrane attack complex C5b-9 have been shown to accumulate in AMD lesions in patients.
source: Complement activation pathways converge on the critical complement component C3, leading to the generation of complement activation products C3a, C5a and the membrane attack complex C5b-9, which have been shown to accumulate in AMD lesions in patients (Johnson et al., 2000; Mullins et al., 2014; Nozaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Complement C3 is found in the retina particularly along Bruch's membrane.
source: Complement C3 is found in the retina particularly along Bruch's membrane and we also observed strong immunolabeling for C3 in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice (Figure 5A), whereas no C3 was detected in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Strong immunolabeling for C3 is observed in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice.
source: Complement C3 is found in the retina particularly along Bruch's membrane and we also observed strong immunolabeling for C3 in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice (Figure 5A), whereas no C3 was detected in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No C3 was detected in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice.
source: Complement C3 is found in the retina particularly along Bruch's membrane and we also observed strong immunolabeling for C3 in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice (Figure 5A), whereas no C3 was detected in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: C5b-9 is detected in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice but not in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice.
source: Consistent with a requirement of C3 for the formation of C5b-9, immunolabeling detected C5b-9 in CNV lesions of Vegfahyper mice but not in CNV lesions of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6-weeks-old VegfahyperC3-/- mice had significantly fewer CNV lesions than age-matched Vegfahyper littermates.
source: We found that 6-weeks-old VegfahyperC3-/- mice had significantly fewer CNV lesions than age-matched Vegfahyper littermates (corresponding to VegfahyperC3+/+ mice without inactivation of C3), but no difference in CNV lesion size was observed (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: No difference in CNV lesion size was observed between VegfahyperC3-/- mice and Vegfahyper littermates.
source: We found that 6-weeks-old VegfahyperC3-/- mice had significantly fewer CNV lesions than age-matched Vegfahyper littermates (corresponding to VegfahyperC3+/+ mice without inactivation of C3), but no difference in CNV lesion size was observed (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: Female Vegfahyper mice tend to have fewer CNV lesions than male Vegfahyper mice.
source: Notably, female Vegfahyper mice tend to have fewer CNV lesions than male Vegfahyper mice (Figures 2C and 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 2C and 4C.

claim: The potent relative reduction in VEGF-A-induced CNV lesion numbers in mice lacking C3 compared to their Vegfahyper littermates was observed only in male mice but not in female mice.
source: However, the potent relative reduction in VEGF-A-induced CNV lesion numbers in mice lacking C3 compared to their Vegfahyper littermates was observed only in male mice but not in female mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Female C57bl6 mice show a reduced ability to promote inflammation via C5b-9, while they show normal complement cascade functionality at the level of C3.
source: This is consistent with the previously reported observation that female C57bl6 mice show a reduced ability to promote inflammation via C5b-9, while they show normal complement cascade functionality at the level of C3 (Kotimaa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kotimaa et al., 2016.

claim: VEGF-A-induced CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice is likely promoted by terminal complement pathway activation.
source: Thus, the difference in CNV lesion numbers between male and female VegfahyperC3-/- mice also suggests that VEGF-A-induced CNV lesion formation in Vegfahyper mice is likely promoted by terminal complement pathway activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the sex-specific effects of C3 deficiency on CNV.

claim: A > 3 fold increase in caspase-1 p10 levels occurs in RPE/choroid lysates of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (lacking complement C3) compared to age-matched WT mice.
source: Importantly, we observed a > 3 fold increase in caspase-1 p10 levels in RPE/choroid lysates of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (lacking complement C3) compared to age-matched WT mice, demonstrating that lack of C3 does not prevent inflammasome activation in these eyes (Figure 5E; ratios of p10/β-actin band intensity quantifications shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Lack of C3 does not prevent inflammasome activation in eyes of VegfahyperC3-/- mice.
source: Importantly, we observed a > 3 fold increase in caspase-1 p10 levels in RPE/choroid lysates of VegfahyperC3-/- mice (lacking complement C3) compared to age-matched WT mice, demonstrating that lack of C3 does not prevent inflammasome activation in these eyes (Figure 5E; ratios of p10/β-actin band intensity quantifications shown).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the western blot data showing p10 in C3-/- mice.

claim: C3 is not required for inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice.
source: However, the findings show that C3 is not required for inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice and that inflammasome activation can occur through C3-independent parallel activation mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the western blot data showing p10 in C3-/- mice.

claim: Inflammasome activation can occur through C3-independent parallel activation mechanisms.
source: However, the findings show that C3 is not required for inflammasome activation in RPE/choroid lysates of Vegfahyper mice and that inflammasome activation can occur through C3-independent parallel activation mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the western blot data showing p10 in C3-/- mice.

claim: C3 affects CNV lesion formation mainly through inflammasome-independent mechanisms.
source: As lack of C3 results in fewer CNV lesions in male VegfahyperC3-/- mice compared to male Vegfahyper mice in a highly significant manner despite inflammasome activation in their RPE/choroids, this suggests that C3 affects CNV lesion formation mainly through inflammasome-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data showing CNV reduction with C3 deficiency despite persistent inflammasome activation.

claim: Vegfahyper mice lacking all inflammasomes (VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice) have fewer CNV lesions than VegfahyperC3-/- mice.
source: This conclusion is also supported by the data showing that Vegfahyper mice lacking all inflammasomes (VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice) have fewer CNV lesions than VegfahyperC3-/- mice (if C3 would be critical for inflammasome activation, then VegfahyperC3-/- mice should have a similarly strong reduction in CNV lesions as VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice) (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CNV lesion induction (CNV numbers) is promoted by complement C3, but not their growth (CNV area).
source: Notably, the observation that CNV lesion induction (CNV numbers) is promoted by complement C3, but not their growth (CNV area) (Figure 5C), was also made when targeting NLRP3 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 5C and 2B-C.

claim: When targeting all inflammasomes (in VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice), a much more potent inhibition of CNV lesion numbers and of their growth (CNV area) is observed.
source: In contrast, when targeting all inflammasomes (in VegfahyperCasp1-/-Casp11-/- mice), we observed not only a much more potent inhibition of CNV lesion numbers but also of their growth (CNV area) (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: CNV lesion growth is at least in part also affected by NLRP3- and C3-independent mechanisms.
source: This suggests that CNV lesion growth is at least in part also affected by NLRP3- and C3-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of targeting NLRP3, C3, or all inflammasomes on CNV area.

claim: C3 inactivation caused no major morphological abnormalities of the RPE or retina when examined at 6 weeks of age.
source: C3 inactivation caused no major morphological abnormalities of the RPE or retina when examined at 6 weeks of age, as assessed by cross-sectional morphology of the RPE and the outer nuclear layer (ONL) as well as by RPE staining of choroidal flat mounts with phalloidin (Figure 5D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figures 5D and F.

claim: RPE cells in C3-/- mice maintain their typical honeycomb pattern morphology even with progressive age.
source: Choroidal flat mounts of 12-months-old C3-/- mice showed that RPE cells maintain their typical honeycomb pattern morphology even with progressive age (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aged C3-/- mice developed retinal abnormalities that were not observed in 6-weeks-old mice.
source: Notably, previously published detailed studies showed that aged C3-/- mice developed retinal abnormalities that were not observed in 6-weeks-old mice, confirming our observation that at the time in which we quantified CNV lesions (6 weeks of age) no RPE/retinal abnormalities could be attributed to C3 deficiency (Hoh Kam et al., 2013; Mukai et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Complement C3 plays a role in the maintenance of retinal function with age progression.
source: While these studies show that complement C3 plays a role in the maintenance of retinal function with age progression, it remains to be shown whether these retinal abnormalities in aged C3-/- mice are a consequence of life-long C3 deficiency and whether targeting C3 or other complement pathway components in aged adults impairs retinal function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited studies showing retinal abnormalities in aged C3-/- mice.

claim: VEGF-A-induced neovascular AMD-like pathologies are promoted through inflammasome activation that occurs predominantly in non-RPE cells.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that VEGF-A-induced neovascular AMD-like pathologies are promoted through inflammasome activation that occurs predominantly in non-RPE cells, and which is only in part mediated by NLRP3 but can also occur independently of NLRP3, caspase-11, or complement C3 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of multiple experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Therapeutic strategies that combine approaches to inhibit both inflammasome activation and complement-mediated inflammation could result in more potent inhibition of neovascular AMD than either treatment approach alone.
source: Thus, therapeutic strategies that combine approaches to inhibit both inflammasome activation and complement-mediated inflammation could result in more potent inhibition of neovascular AMD than either treatment approach alone.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the finding that complement and inflammasomes act through independent mechanisms.

claim: The increase in VEGF-A levels occurs in Vegfahyper mice as a consequence of the heterozygous insertion of an IRES-NLS-lacZ-SV40pA sequence +202 bp 3' to the STOP codon into the 3-'UTR of the Vegfa gene locus.
source: The increase in VEGF-A levels occurs in these mice as a consequence of the heterozygous insertion of an IRES-NLS-lacZ-SV40pA sequence +202 bp 3' to the STOP codon into the 3-'UTR of the Vegfa gene locus (Miquerol et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miquerol et al., 1999.

claim: The observed ocular abnormalities in Vegfahyper mice always co-segregated with the Vegfahyper allele (VegfalacZ/WT) and were not observed in any of the examined control littermate mice.
source: The observed ocular abnormalities always co-segregated with the Vegfahyper allele (VegfalacZ/WT) and were not observed in any of the examined control littermate mice (Ablonczy et al., 2014; Marneros, 2013; Marneros, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Mice lacking Casp1 have an incidental Casp11 mutation, rendering them double KOs for both caspase-1 and caspase-11.
source: Of note, mice lacking Casp1 have an incidental Casp11 mutation (Casp1 and Casp11 are too close in the genome to be segregated by recombination), rendering them double KOs for both caspase-1 and caspase-11 (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: Casp11 null mice have a functional Casp1 gene.
source: In contrast, Casp11 null mice have a functional Casp1 gene.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the genetic characteristics of these mouse strains.

claim: Casp1-/-/Casp11-/- mice and Casp11-/- mice have both been shown to lack functional caspase-11 protein.
source: Casp1-/-/Casp11-/- mice and Casp11-/- mice have both been shown to lack functional caspase-11 protein (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: Homozygous Nlrp3A350V mice contain a floxed neo cassette in reverse orientation (neoR) in intron 2 leading to the lack of functional Nlrp3 gene expression in the absence of Cre expression.
source: Homozygous Nlrp3A350V mice contain a floxed neo cassette in reverse orientation (neoR) in intron 2 leading to the lack of functional Nlrp3 gene expression in the absence of Cre expression (here referred to as Nlrp3-/- mice) (Brydges et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brydges et al., 2009.

claim: Cre recombinase expression in Best1Cre/+ mice occurs specifically in RPE cells and not in other cells of the eye.
source: The specificity of Cre recombinase expression in Best1Cre/+ mice has been extensively analyzed previously, and it was shown both in eye sections as well as in choroidal flat mounts that Cre recombinase expression in the eyes of these mice occurs specifically in RPE cells and not in other cells of the eye (Iacovelli et al., 2011), which we confirmed in our previous study as well (He et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice Best1Cre/+-mediated removal of the floxed neoR cassette in intron 2 of the Nlrp3 gene occurs only in RPE cells.
source: We also confirmed that in VegfahyperBest1Cre/+Nlrp3A350V/A350V mice Best1Cre/+-mediated removal of the floxed neoR cassette in intron 2 of the Nlrp3 gene indeed occurs only in RPE cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data showing Cre-mediated excision only in RPE cells.
